newsitem.title: USA: Hoffa name an asset in bid for Teamster presidency.
newsitem.headline: Hoffa name an asset in bid for Teamster presidency.

text.p: One thing Jimmy Hoffa does not have to worry about in his bid to become president of the Teamsters Union is name recognition.
As the son and namesake of the most well-known figure in the union and perhaps the entire labour movement, James P. Hoffa can afford to stress broader themes in the bitter race.
"The campaign is not about the Hoffa name," he said recently. "It is about the Teamsters Union. It is about members taking back their union, restoring respect to the union."
Hoffa's father, James R. Hoffa, made a name for himself as the tough-guy leader of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters during its heyday of the 1950s and 1960s.

In the summer of 1975 he became a Teamster legend when he vanished mysteriously. He is presumed to have been murdered while plotting to recapture the union presidency he was forced to give up as a condition for his early release from prison.

While the younger Hoffa, 55, is not shy about mentioning his father and says the name has been an asset more often than not ("95 percent, I'll take that"), he has sought to focus his campaign on his opponent, union President Ron Carey.

"The debate in this election is a referendum on his past five years," he said in an interview. "This man has single-handedly brought the largest, richest union in the free world to the edge of bankruptcy."
Carey, 60, a self-styled reformer and former dissident leader of a New York local, won the union's presidency in a three-way race in 1991 that was open to all Teamster members.
That was not the way the Teamsters did business in Hoffa's father's day. Until 1991, presidents of what was once America's biggest union -- it's now No. 2 -- were chosen at conventions.

But in a 1989 settlement of a federal racketeering suit, the union that for years symbolised labour corruption -- four of six past presidents were imprisoned or indicted -- agreed to elect leaders in government-run, rank-and-file elections.
Ballots will be mailed to all 1.4 million Teamster members on Nov. 8. They will have about a month to send them back.
Hoffa, who bears a noticeable resemblance to his father, clearly revels in the rituals of campaigning.

At a rally last weekend in North Bergen, N.J., where he was greeted by bagpipers, he beamed a bright smile as he posed for pictures with supporters, autographed their clothes and stirred them up with denunciations of the man he hopes to unseat.
"Are you gonna help me kick Ron Carey's ass?" he asked, as they roared their approval and chanted "Hoffa, Hoffa, Hoffa."
Hoffa described Carey as a phony, corrupt, inept, vindictive stooge for the union's government overseers.

Spinning a hypothetical scenario of Justice Department officials, employers and "international capitalists who were plotting to destroy the Teamsters union," Hoffa tells the crowd that such conspirators would want to install "a guy like Ron Carey," drain the union's assets, deplete its strike fund, stop organising new members and create disunity among its locals.
"The five things that Ron Carey's done is exactly what the enemies of this union want," he says.

Carey blames the union's financial woes on lavish spending by his predecessors. He cites a 1991 convention decision to raise strike pay to $200 a week from $55 without providing a way to fund the increase as the reason the strike fund went bust after a three-week national truck strike in 1994.
A key plank in Hoffa's platform is to boost strike pay to four times a members' monthly dues, up to $250 a week, in part by diverting $15 million from the union's general funds.
With both candidates vowing not to raise dues, Carey says the Hoffa plan would gut services. Hoffa insists he can cut fat and waste, without cutting services.
Another issue in the race that has been marred with mutual mud-slinging is corruption. Each candidate accuses the other.
Carey has placed 66 locals under temporary trusteeships, mostly because of corruption charges. But Hoffa says the tactic has been used as a vendetta against Carey's enemies.
One local officer ousted by Carey is Hoffa's former running mate for the union's No. 2 spot, Bill Hogan. He says he pulled out of the race to avoid hurting Hoffa and denies the charges.
"There are stories all over this union of people who got thrown out of office because they wouldn't dance to someone else's music," Hogan said. "And I'm just one of those stories."
Hoffa says it is Carey who is corrupt and accuses federal officials of going easy on him and his allies. He cites a 1987 immunity deal between Carey and federal prosecutors.
For his part, Hoffa admitted he once invested in a limited partnership that included a mob figure, but withdrew when he learned of his participation.
Hoffa worked under a Teamster contract only briefly before becoming a labour lawyer. Since 1993, he has worked for Teamster Joint Council 43 in Detroit, once headed by his father.
But he is adamant about his Teamster ties.
"All my life I've been going to union meetings," he told the rally. "That is my heritage. And by God, don't anybody ever question my credibility or my commitment to this union."
The name comes in handy too.
"You must be the real Jimmy Hoffa," a supporter told him.
"I am, man," he responded.
